text: A single log entry rarely tells the whole story -- an attacker's actions are scattered across a firewall, a few servers, some endpoints, maybe an application. Getting the real picture takes three steps, in order: aggregation pulls those logs into one place, normalization makes them comparable, and correlation combines them into a pattern. Skip or reorder any of those three, and the other two don't work.

Aggregation is the simplest of the three: pull logs from firewalls, Windows and Linux servers, endpoint agents, and applications into one central system, instead of leaving an analyst to log into a dozen consoles separately. Normalization comes next -- and it has to come next, because every vendor formats its logs differently. Only after logs share a common schema can anything downstream treat a Windows event and a Cisco firewall event as the same kind of thing.

A Windows Event Log records a failed logon as EventID 4625 with its own field names; a Cisco ASA firewall logs the same source address under a completely different syslog format; a Palo Alto firewall formats it differently still. Normalization maps each of those into one shared schema -- so 'source IP' means the same field no matter which vendor wrote the original line. Real schemas like Common Event Format and the Elastic Common Schema exist to solve exactly this problem.

Only once events are normalized does correlation actually work. Say System A logs a failed login attempt at 10:02 AM. A minute later, System B logs a successful login -- from that same source IP address. Neither event alone is remarkable; failed logins and successful logins both happen constantly. Correlated together, they become one incident with a working theory: someone testing stolen credentials, or an attacker moving laterally after a first foothold.
Next lesson draws a sharper line: a tool that just stores and searches logs isn't automatically a SIEM. What correlation and alerting add on top is the real difference.
